lead: Fargo sits on the flat Red River Valley, where the river flows north and spring floods are a way of life. Snowmelt, river flooding and deep cold drive most of its water damage.
risk: spring river flooding, basement water and frozen pipes
why: The Red River flows north toward Canada, so its upper reaches often thaw while the river downstream is still frozen. Water backs up and spreads across the flat valley. In March 2009, the river crested at a record of nearly 41 feet in Fargo. Thousands of volunteers filled sandbags to save the city. Big floods also hit in 1997 and 2011, and a large diversion channel is being built to protect Fargo and Moorhead.

Even in years without a big flood, spring snowmelt soaks the clay soil and pushes water into basements. Most Fargo homes have them, and sump pumps run hard every spring. Winters are among the coldest of any U.S. city. Pipes in outside walls, crawl spaces and garages freeze and split, and the leaks often show up days later when the pipe thaws.
image_alt: Flooded fields along a dirt road under a clear sky
image_caption: Spring snowmelt and Red River flooding are a yearly worry in Fargo.
problems: Homes near the Red River, Rose Creek
Homes with older pumps and pits
tips: Test your sump pump before the spring thaw and add a backup.
Move snow away from the foundation before it melts.
Check your flood risk even if you are not on the river.
Insulate pipes on outside walls and keep heat on when away.
areas: Calls come from Downtown, Hawthorne, Roosevelt, Horace Mann, Clara Barton, Osgood, Rose Creek and Jefferson, plus West Fargo, Moorhead and Horace.

faq.q: When should I buy flood insurance in Fargo?
faq.a: Before the snow starts to melt. NFIP policies usually take 30 days to start, and you cannot wait until a flood forecast comes out. Even homes outside the mapped zone can see water in a big year. Check your coverage for both the building and your belongings.
